text: Evening. Frank DeLuca, DeLuca Hardware on Fifth. My grandfather opened it in 1951. He came over with eleven words of English and his papers in order, and he waited his turn. Nobody ever had to come looking for him. $ Look, I know people are scared, and I don't like it. Two agents came into my store asking about a kid who used to sweep for me, and I didn't enjoy that. But a country has rules, and people who follow the rules have nothing to fear. I'm not going to stand at my counter and tell forty kids who did it the right way that the rules don't matter. $ My grandfather did it the right way. I'd like that to still mean something.

_to the moderator_ What should the next governor do first? One set of rules, the same for everybody, and fast. Nobody should wait ten years for an answer. That's not fair to the ones waiting or the ones who already waited. $ Second, free English classes, nights and weekends, with a job at the end. I've hired forty kids in thirty years, and the ones who sound like they're from here get the call back. I'm not saying that's nice. I'm saying I've seen it. $ And stop splitting this town into programs, one for this group and one for that one. Come to the merchants' breakfast. Bagels, bad coffee, everybody at one table, in English. That's how my grandfather got to be from here.

Evening. Frank DeLuca, DeLuca Hardware on Fifth, since 1951. $ The city tells me I need my safety signs in four languages now. Fine, they're up; I don't argue with a fire inspector. But look, I'm told all this is about welcome. My grandfather wasn't welcomed. He was expected. Expected to learn the language, show up, get on with it. He did, my father did, I did. $ Now there's a grant and a festival and a form in your own language for everybody, and nobody asks anybody to become American anymore. Something we share is getting lost, and I worry about that. If you came to America, why not become American? That's not an insult. It's an invitation.

_to the moderator_ What should the next governor do first? Spend it on English, not on interpreters. An interpreter helps you once. English helps you every day for the rest of your life, at the bank, at the counter, at parents' night. $ Make the citizenship test the finish line, and make the line short. I'll sponsor the pencils; I already do. $ And let a town be a town, not a map of who's from where. My Little League team, the parents in the stands speak six languages. On the field it's one word: run. Nobody on that field cares where your parents came from. I'd like the whole town to work like that field.
Now that's somebody from here. Come by the store and I'll introduce you around Fifth.
Both is fine at home, sure. Just make sure the town hears the English half. That's all I ask.
Look, every group in its own corner is how you end up with a town of corners. My grandfather moved to Fifth for a reason.
Fair enough. Listening's underrated. Most people at these things are just waiting for their turn.
Takes nerve to get up there. You did all right.
